name: Persepolis
info: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, a palace complex on a walled terrace in the plains of Marvdasht in Fars, Iran, built from about 515 BCE and burned after Alexander took it in 330 BCE.

facts.founded: The earliest remains date to 515 BCE; Darius I built the terrace and the palaces, and the French archaeologist André Godard believed that Cyrus the Great had chosen the site.
facts.where: On a terrace leaning on Rahmat Mountain, near the small river Pulvar, in the plains of Marvdasht, encircled by the southern Zagros Mountains, in Fars province of Iran.
facts.known: The Apadana and its stairway reliefs; the Gate of All Nations; the Hundred-Columns Palace; the Tachara and Hadish palaces; the burning of the palaces in 330 BCE; the Persepolis Fortification Archive; the trilingual royal inscriptions that helped the decipherment of cuneiform
facts.today: Persepolis is a ruin and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Fars province, Iran.

t: Persepolis was raised on a great terrace by Darius I from about 519 to 515 BCE, and Xerxes I and later kings added to it until the downfall of the Achaemenid Empire.
It was a ceremonial complex used seasonally rather than one of the largest cities of the empire, and its function, including where the king's private quarters stood, is still not entirely clear.
Alexander the Great took it in 330 BCE, and soon afterwards its wooden parts were destroyed by fire; its ruins were visited by European travellers from the 15th century and excavated from 1930.
dyk: The study of the trilingual royal inscriptions found on the ruins of Persepolis led to the initial decipherment of cuneiform in the early 19th century.
ev: Construction of the broad stairway of the terrace begins
Date of the earliest remains and of the coin hoard laid under the foundation boxes of the Apadana
Darius I dies, and Xerxes I completes the Tachara palace
Alexander the Great takes Persepolis, and a fire destroys its palaces
Persepolis is still the capital of Persia as a province of the Macedonian Empire
The Sasanian prince Shapur Sakanshah leaves an inscription naming the site Sad-stun
García de Silva Figueroa links Chehel Minar with the Persepolis of the classical authors
Ernst Herzfeld and Erich Schmidt begin the first scientific excavations

sections.origins:
Persepolis stands in the plains of Marvdasht, encircled by the southern Zagros Mountains, in Fars province of Iran. It lies near the small river Pulvar, which flows into the Kur River. The site includes a terrace of 125,000 m2, partly artificially constructed and partly cut out of a mountain, with its east side leaning on Rahmat Mountain. Archaeological evidence shows that the earliest remains date back to 515 BCE, and construction of a broad stairway was begun around 519 BCE.

André Godard, the French archaeologist who excavated Persepolis in the early 1930s, believed that Cyrus the Great chose the site but that Darius I built the terrace and the palaces, and inscriptions on the buildings support the belief that Darius constructed them. His work ran parallel to that of the Palace of Susa, which according to Gene R. Garthwaite served as his model. Ernst Herzfeld held that the reasons for building were the need for a majestic atmosphere, a symbol for the empire and a place to celebrate special events, especially Nowruz, and that it was built where the Achaemenid dynasty had been founded, although it was not the centre of the empire at that time.

In 2011 an Italian-Iranian team found a gateway of 40 by 30 metres at Tol-e Ajori, 3 km west of Persepolis, resembling the Ishtar Gate of Babylon. The excavators concluded that it was older than Persepolis, built between the conquest of Babylon in 539 and the start of construction in 518 BCE.
sections.growth:
Darius I ordered the construction of the Apadana and the Council Hall (the Tripylon, or Triple Gate), as well as the main imperial Treasury and its surroundings. These were completed in the reign of his son Xerxes I, and further building on the terrace continued until the downfall of the Achaemenid Empire. Grey limestone was the main building material. The uneven plan of the terrace acted like a castle, its angled walls enabling defenders to target any section of the external front.

The Apadana, on the western side of the platform, was the greatest palace and was used by the King of Kings for official audiences. Foundation tablets of gold and silver found in two deposition boxes beneath it carry an inscription of Darius in Old Persian cuneiform that describes his kingdom as stretching from the Sacae beyond Sogdia to Kush, and from the Indus valley to Lydia. Beneath the boxes lay a hoard of coins dated to about 515 BCE.

The Throne Hall, also called the Hundred-Columns Palace, measured 70 by 70 metres. Xerxes I started it and his son Artaxerxes I completed it by the end of the fifth century BCE. Tachara, the palace of Darius, was completed after his death in 486 BCE by Xerxes, who called it a Taçara, Old Persian for "winter palace". The Hadish Palace of Xerxes covers 2,550 square metres on the highest level of the terrace. The buildings fall into three groups: military quarters, the treasury, and the reception halls and occasional houses of the king.
sections.rulers:
Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, which lasted from about 550 to 330 BCE. With Darius I the sceptre passed to a new branch of the royal house, and the country's true capitals were Susa, Babylon and Ecbatana. This may be why the Greeks were not acquainted with the city until Alexander the Great took and plundered it. Inscriptions at Persepolis, eleven in all, relate to Darius, Xerxes, Artaxerxes II and Artaxerxes III, and a palace of Artaxerxes III stands on the terrace.

Behind the compound three tombs were cut into the rock of the hillside. It is commonly accepted that Cyrus the Great was buried in his tomb at Pasargadae. The kings buried at Naqsh-e Rostam were probably Darius I, Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I and Darius II, and the two completed graves behind Persepolis would then belong to Artaxerxes II and Artaxerxes III. To whom the unfinished tomb, a kilometre from the city, belongs is debated.

After Alexander's conquest in 330 BCE, Persepolis was still the capital of Persia as a province of the Macedonian Empire in 316 BCE, according to Diodorus Siculus. The city must have declined gradually. Estakhr nearby gained prominence as a separate city very shortly after the decline of Persepolis, and much of the rubble of Persepolis appears to have been used to build it.
sections.life:
The exact function of Persepolis remains unclear. It was not one of the largest cities in ancient Iran, let alone in the empire, but appears to have been a grand ceremonial complex occupied only seasonally, raised high on a walled platform with five palaces or halls of varying size and grand entrances. It is still not entirely clear where the king's private quarters were. Until recently most archaeologists held that it was used chiefly for celebrating Nowruz, the Persian New Year, at the spring equinox. The Iranian nobility and the tributary parts of the empire came to present gifts to the king, as the stairway reliefs show. These reliefs allow one to observe people from across the empire in their traditional dress, and the king himself, down to the smallest detail.

It is also unclear what permanent structures stood outside the palace complex, which is why Persepolis is more often called a complex than a city in the usual sense. The lower city at the foot of the terrace might have survived for a longer time. At the beginning of the reign of Xerxes I the Throne Hall was used mainly for receptions for military commanders and representatives of the subject nations, and later it served as an imperial museum.

The Persepolis Fortification Archive records the administration of the place. A damaged tablet from it, dating to around 500 BCE, records the distribution of at least 600 quarts of an unidentified commodity among five villages, and is rare evidence that Old Persian was also used for everyday administration.
sections.crises:
After invading Achaemenid Persia in 330 BCE, Alexander the Great sent the main force of his army to Persepolis by the Royal Road. He stormed the Persian Gates, a pass through the Zagros Mountains, where Ariobarzanes of Persis ambushed his army and inflicted heavy casualties. After being held off for 31 days, Alexander outflanked and destroyed the defenders. Ariobarzanes was killed either during the battle or in the retreat to Persepolis. After several months Alexander allowed his troops to loot Persepolis, and around that time a fire burned the palaces. Diodorus Siculus wrote that the Macedonians slaughtered the men they met and plundered the houses.

It is believed that the fire started in the Hadish Palace, the living quarters of Xerxes I, and spread. It is not clear whether it was an accident or deliberate revenge for the burning of the Acropolis of Athens in the second Persian invasion of Greece. Plutarch, Diodorus and Quintus Curtius Rufus, writing much later, tell that Thaïs, an Athenian, proposed it during a drunken celebration, and that she or Alexander started the fire. The fire may also have aimed to destroy a symbol of the Persian monarchy that could have become a focus of resistance.

The Zoroastrian Book of Arda Wiraz says the archives of Persepolis held all the Avesta and Zend, written on cow-skins in gold ink, and that they were destroyed. The fire did not damage the Fortification Archive tablets but may have caused the upper part of the northern fortification wall to collapse, which preserved them.
sections.legacy:
The Greek name Persepolis is a compound of Pérsēs and pólis, "the city of the Persians". The ancient Persians called the city Pārsa, also the word for the region of Persia. An inscription of 311 CE by the Sasanian prince Shapur Sakanshah names the site Sad-stun, "Hundred Pillars". Medieval Persians attributed it to Jamshid, a king of Iranian mythology, and called it Takht-e Jamshid, and also Chehel Minar, "Forty Minarets".

Visitors described the ruins from the 15th century. Giosafat Barbaro visited in 1474, and in 1618 García de Silva Figueroa was the first Western traveller to link Chehel Minar with the Persepolis of the classical authors. Pietro Della Valle noticed in 1621 that only 25 of the 72 original columns still stood. The exploration of the site from the early 17th century led to the modern rediscovery of cuneiform and, through studies of the trilingual royal inscriptions, to its initial decipherment in the early 19th century. Ernst Herzfeld and Erich Schmidt of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago excavated for eight seasons from 1930.

Today the ruins of colossal buildings of dark-grey marble stand on the terrace. Fifteen pillars are intact and three more have been re-erected since 1970. Reliefs and other objects are held by the British Museum, the Oriental Institute in Chicago and other museums. In 1971 the site was the main staging ground of the celebration of 2,500 years of the Persian Empire under Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. Persepolis is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the key Iranian cultural heritage sites.

summary: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, a complex of palaces on a walled terrace in Fars, begun by Darius I around 519 BCE. Alexander the Great took it in 330 BCE, and fire destroyed its palaces. Its ruins are a World Heritage Site.

END: the article gives no end date for Persepolis as a city. I used 330 BCE (Alexander's taking and the fire). It also says the city was still the capital of Persia in 316 BCE and 'must have gradually declined'; the lower city may have survived longer. Editor may prefer end null-free alternatives.
The article itself treats Persepolis as a complex more than a city; the text says so in 'life'.
